screens.body:
A use case is a story about how someone achieves a goal using your system. It has three ingredients: an actor (who), a goal (what they want), and the steps (how it happens).

Example from your world: on SwiftGigs, "Post a task" — the actor is the task poster, the goal is getting help, and the steps are: open the app, describe the task, set the budget, publish. That story IS the use case.

options: A story of an actor achieving a goal in steps
check.question: A use case is…

screens.heading: Stories, not just diagrams

screens.body:
An actor is anyone — or anything — OUTSIDE the system that interacts with it. Usually a person (customer, admin), but it can be another system too, like a payment service or a notification provider.

The trick: name actors by their ROLE, not by a person's name. "Task poster" beats "Morolake," because the role stays true even when the person changes. One human can play several actor roles.

options: Anyone/anything outside the system that interacts with it, named by role
The main character in a movie
check.question: An actor is…

screens.heading: Who are the actors?
screens.keyPoint: Outside the system, named by role.

screens.body:
A well-written use case has a shape: a name ("Post a task"), the actor, preconditions (what must already be true — "user is logged in"), the main flow (the happy-path steps, numbered), alternate flows (what if something goes wrong), and postconditions (what's true when it ends — "task is visible to earners").

The alternate flows are where the real thinking happens. "What if the payment fails?" asked now is a design decision; asked after launch is a crisis.

options: Name, actor, preconditions, main flow, alternates, postconditions
Just a title and a doodle
check.question: A complete use case includes…

screens.heading: Anatomy of a use case

screens.body:
A use case diagram draws the big picture: stick figures for actors, ovals for use cases, lines connecting who can do what. At a glance, the whole system's scope becomes visible.

Two special relationships show up: «include» (one use case always uses another — "Post a task" includes "Log in") and «extend» (an optional add-on — "Apply promo code" extends "Pay for task"). They keep the diagram tidy instead of repeating steps everywhere.

options: Actors, use cases, and their connections — with include/extend for reuse
check.question: A use case diagram shows…

screens.heading: The diagram view
screens.keyPoint: Actors, ovals, lines — the system's scope at a glance.

screens.body:
A sequence diagram zooms into ONE use case and shows the conversation over time. Time flows downward; each participant gets a vertical "lifeline," and arrows between them are messages: who calls whom, in what order.

Posting a task might read: Poster → App: "submit task" → App → Server: "save task" → Server → Database: "insert row" → Database → Server: "saved!" You can literally trace a request's journey.

options: The ordered messages between participants in one scenario
check.question: A sequence diagram shows…

screens.heading: Sequence diagrams: the conversation
screens.keyPoint: Time goes down; arrows show who talks to whom.

screens.body:
Reading one is a superpower for developers: start at the top, follow each arrow down, and ask "does my code do exactly this, in this order?" Mismatches between the diagram and the code are bugs waiting to happen.

They also expose hidden complexity. If one simple use case needs fourteen messages across six participants, maybe the design is doing too much — and that's cheaper to discover on paper than in code.

options: Trace each message top-to-bottom and compare with the code
Count the arrows and pick the biggest number
check.question: To read a sequence diagram:

screens.heading: Reading them like a developer
screens.keyPoint: Top to bottom, arrow by arrow.

screens.body:
All of this — use cases, diagrams — is UML, the Unified Modeling Language: a shared visual vocabulary for describing software. When everyone draws the same way, a diagram drawn in Calgary reads the same in Lagos.

Models are thinking tools, not paperwork. Their job is to catch misunderstandings while they're still cheap — a confused arrow costs nothing; a confused codebase costs weeks.

options: A shared visual language for describing software designs
check.question: UML is…

screens.heading: Why model at all
screens.keyPoint: Catch confusion on paper, not in code.

screens.body: OMG (omg.org) maintains the official UML specification — the source of truth for every diagram shape. AgileModeling.com (Scott Ambler) offers practical, plain-spoken guidance on modeling well. The Scrum Guide (scrum.org) shows where these analysis artifacts fit in an agile workflow.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The UML spec lives at omg.org.
